summary: A humorous article recounting five comic salt block grilling mishaps by rookie grillers in autumn 2023, each illustrating a common mistake: heating too fast, cooking fatty meat, stacking blocks, over-seasoning, and washing the block. It frames the mishaps as lessons on caution and respect when using Himalayan salt blocks, ending on a light note that laughter is the best seasoning.
one_line: A comic roundup of five rookie salt block grilling disasters in 2023, each showing a common mistake and its lesson.
key_facts: Salt block grilling cooks food on a large slab of Himalayan salt, which adds a subtle savory flavor and provides even heat distribution.
On October 18, 2023, Joe "Sizzle King" Thompson of Flavorville put a new salt block over a roaring flame, and it cracked down the center because salt blocks must be preheated slowly.
On December 5, 2023, Becky "BBQ Queen" Reynolds grilled fatty ribs on a salt block, which soaked up the grease and caused a flare-up in her backyard; the ribs ended up like charcoal briquettes.
On November 23, 2023, Gregory Anderson built a tower of multiple salt blocks at the Anderson family reunion; it became unstable like Jenga and collapsed, sending shrimp flying.
On September 30, 2023, Sandra "Season-It-All" Jenkins coated salmon fillets with heavy herbs and spices on the salt block, making the fish overly salty.
Sandra Jenkins's dinner guests were last seen reaching for water glasses after eating the over-seasoned salmon.
On November 17, 2023, Derek "I Didn't Touch It" Simmons washed his salt block before serving, and it began dissolving and shrinking.
Derek Simmons's pork loin dinner was passed off to guests as a "deconstructed" pork dinner after his salt block dissolved.
The article says the salt block grilling trend caught on among gourmet adventurists after September 2023.
The article's lessons: preheat slowly, avoid fatty meats, keep stacks stable, go easy on added seasoning, and never wash the block with water.
